old:
Should carer support be judged by whether it delays a care home move?

In a UK trial, 260 family carers of people with dementia were chosen by chance to have an eight-session coping programme (START) or usual care. Over six years of follow-up, carers who had the programme had fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression. The average difference was modest. The trial did not show a clear difference in how soon the person with dementia moved into a care home, and the range of results was wide.

A separate US trial of 406 spouse carers of people with Alzheimer disease linked counselling and support with a later nursing home move for the person with the disease: a model estimated the difference in median time at about 18 months.

The two differ in people, era and design, so they should not be ranked against each other. We should judge carer support first by the carer's own health and quality of life.

More posts in the What gets counted series ask what services measure and what people value.

old:
Should carer support be judged by whether it delays a care home move?

Two trials of programmes for family carers of people with dementia looked at different outcomes in different people.

In the UK START trial, 260 family carers were chosen by chance to have an eight-session coping programme or usual care. Over six years the programme left carers with fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression (an adjusted average difference of 2 points on a 42-point scale, which is modest). Care home admission was a secondary outcome. The trial did not show a clear difference in how soon the person with dementia moved into a care home, and the range of results was wide, so that is not evidence of no effect.

In a US trial of 406 spouse carers of people with Alzheimer disease, counselling and support was linked with a later nursing home move for the person with the disease. A model estimated the difference in median time at about 18 months (557 days).

The two trials differ in people, era and programme, so they should not be compared head to head. Counted only by care home admission, START would look like a failure although carers benefited.

Our judgement, not a finding: we should judge carer support first by the carer's own health and quality of life. A later care home move is not automatically a better outcome, and an earlier one is not automatically a failure.

More posts in the What gets counted series ask what services measure and what people value.
